**GitHub repo:** <https://github.com/yourusername/ec422_ps3_cachoua>

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)

retail_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/retail_sales_raw.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    RSAFS = col_double(),
    RSAFSNA = col_double()
  )
)
```

## Time and Tsibbles

The retail data comes from FRED and is from the Census Bureau's monthly retail trade survey. RSAFS is seasonally adjusted retail and food services sales and RSAFSNA is the same thing but not seasonally adjusted. Both are monthly and in millions of dollars, starting in January 1992. In `retail_ts` the index is `Month` and the key is `series_id`. The `can_gas` data comes from the `canadian_gas` dataset in fpp3. It is monthly natural gas production in Canada in billions of cubic meters from 1960 to February 2005. Its index is `Month` and it has no key since there is only one series.

### Reading dates (2.2)

```{r}
head(read_csv("data/retail_sales_raw.csv", show_col_types = FALSE))
```

2.2a: The `observation_date` column is read in as `<date>`, so read_csv guessed it right.

### Long format and the tsibble (2.3 to 2.4)

```{r}
retail_raw_long <- retail_raw |>
  select(observation_date, RSAFS, RSAFSNA) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(RSAFS, RSAFSNA), names_to = "series_id", values_to = "sales")

head(retail_raw_long)

retail_ts <- retail_raw_long |>
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(observation_date)) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = series_id)

head(retail_ts)
has_gaps(retail_ts)
```

The header says [1M] so it is monthly, and has_gaps() is FALSE for both series so there are no gaps.

### Canadian gas (2.5)

```{r}
key_vars(canadian_gas)
index_var(canadian_gas)

can_gas <- canadian_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume)

has_gaps(can_gas)
head(can_gas)
```

### Working with dates (2.6)

```{r}
can_gas_recent <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month >= yearmonth("1990 Jan")) |>
  mutate(year    = year(Month),
         month   = month(Month, label = TRUE),
         quarter = quarter(Month))

can_gas_recent |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(avg_volume = mean(Volume)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

2.6b: December has the highest average production (17.1) and June has the lowest (14.9).

```{r}
can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(next_month           = Month + 1,
         same_month_last_year = Month - 12) |>
  head()
```

```{r}
can_gas_q <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2004 Dec")) |>
  index_by(Quarter = yearquarter(Month)) |>
  summarize(Volume = sum(Volume))

head(can_gas_q)
can_gas_q |> autoplot(Volume) + theme_minimal()
```

2.6d: We use sum because each month's value is how much gas was produced that month, so adding the three months gives the total for the quarter. The mean would just give the average month. The quarterly series still looks seasonal since it goes up and down in the same pattern every year.

### Plotting with autoplot() (2.7)

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales",
    subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

2.7b: The NSA series spikes up every December, probably from holiday shopping, and then drops in January and February. The SA series does not have these spikes and is much smoother. Over the long run both series follow the same path. They both trend up and both show the drops in 2008 and 2020, so seasonal adjustment doesn't seem to change the trend or the recessions.

```{r}
can_gas |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Canadian Natural Gas Production",
    subtitle = "Monthly, January 1960 to February 2005",
    x = NULL, y = "Billions of cubic meters"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales with Smoothed Trend",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

2.7d: I added geom_smooth() to the retail plot to show the overall trend line without the monthly ups and downs.

## Transformations

### Logs (3.1)

3.1a: The seasonal swings in can_gas get bigger as the series grows from the 1960s through the 1980s. After about 1990 the series keeps growing but the swings actually get smaller, so it's not true for the whole sample.

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(log_volume = log(Volume))

can_gas |>
  autoplot(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Log of Canadian Gas Production", x = NULL, y = "log(Volume)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

3.1b: After taking logs the fast growth in the 1960s is flattened out and the trend looks more curved, growing fast early and then leveling off. The seasonal swings in the early years now look about the same size as the 1980s, but the swings after 1990 still look smaller. I think logs are a decent idea for can_gas because they help with the early years, but they don't fix the smaller swings at the end.

```{r}
retail_nsa <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  mutate(log_sales = log(sales))

retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(title = "NSA Retail Sales (Level)", x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()

retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(log_sales) +
  labs(title = "NSA Retail Sales (Log)", x = NULL, y = "log(sales)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

3.1c: The case for logs is stronger for retail sales because the seasonal swings keep getting bigger as sales grow, and after logging they look about the same size the whole time.

### Growth rates (3.2)

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(
    growth_direct = 100 * difference(Volume) / lag(Volume),
    growth_logdiff = 100 * difference(log_volume),
    growth_gap = abs(growth_direct - growth_logdiff)
  )

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_direct) +
  labs(title = "Canadian Gas Production: Month-over-Month Growth",
       x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)") +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_gap) +
  labs(title = "Gap Between Direct and Log-Difference Growth Rates",
       x = NULL, y = "Absolute difference") +
  theme_minimal()
```

3.2a: The approximation is pretty good here since the gap is usually under half a percentage point, and it's only bigger in the months where growth was really large.

### SA vs. NSA growth (3.3)

```{r}
retail_ts <- retail_ts |>
  group_by_key() |>
  mutate(growth_mom = 100 * difference(log(sales))) |>
  ungroup()

retail_ts |>
  autoplot(growth_mom) +
  labs(
    title = "Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales",
    x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

3.3: The NSA growth rate is a lot noisier than the SA growth rate. NSA jumps up around 15 to 20 percent in December and then falls around 20 to 25 percent in January because of the holiday pattern from 2.7b. The SA growth rate stays close to zero except for big events like 2020.

## Seasonality

### Season plots (4.1)

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales", y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales", y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()
```

4.1b: In the NSA plot every year has the same shape, low in January and February and highest in December. In the SA plot the lines are basically flat across the year, so the seasonal pattern has been removed.

```{r}
can_gas |>
  gg_season(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in Canadian Gas Production", y = "log(Volume)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

4.1c: Gas production is highest in the winter months like December and January and lowest in the summer from June to September. This makes sense because natural gas is used a lot for heating, so people need more of it in the winter.

### Subseries plot (4.2)

```{r}
can_gas |>
  gg_subseries(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production", y = "log(Volume)")
```

### X-13ARIMA-SEATS (4.3)

```{r}
retail_nsa_x13 <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  model(x13 = X_13ARIMA_SEATS(sales)) |>
  components()

retail_nsa_x13 |> autoplot()
```

4.3a: The seasonal factor is highest in December, at around 1.15, so December sales are about 15% above trend. The swings get a little smaller over time, since the December factor goes from about 1.2 in the 1990s to about 1.1 in recent years.

```{r}
sa_compare <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, mine = season_adjust) |>
  left_join(
    retail_ts |>
      filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
      as_tibble() |>
      transmute(Month, census = sales),
    by = "Month"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (log(mine) - log(census)))

sa_compare |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = pct_diff)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's",
       x = NULL, y = "Difference (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

4.3b: My adjustment is pretty close to the official one. Most months are within a few tenths of a percent. The biggest differences are after 2020, especially in January, where mine is up to almost 2% higher.

### Linear trend + seasonal dummies (4.4)

```{r}
can_gas_fit <- can_gas |>
  model(TSLM(log_volume ~ trend() + season()))

can_gas_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

4.4a: The trend coefficient is 0.004, so gas production grew about 0.4% per month on average. June has the most significant seasonal effect, with a t-statistic of about -4.78.

```{r}
can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = log_volume, color = "Actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, color = "Fitted")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

4.4b: The fitted line gets the general upward direction and the seasonal timing, but it misses a lot because the real series is curved and the fitted trend is a straight line. It is too low in the 1970s, too high in the 1980s, and too high again after 2000.

```{r}
can_gas_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()

can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

4.4c: The residuals do not look like white noise. They move in long waves over time and the ACF is high at every lag. The Ljung-Box p-value is 0, so we reject the null of no autocorrelation at the 5% level.

## Forecast Evaluation

### Expanding window (5.1)

```{r}
gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |>
  select(.model, MAE, RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

5.1a: The first forecast evaluated is January 1980 and the last one is February 2005. The seasonal naive model is more accurate, with an MAE of 0.56 compared to 4.01 for the TSLM and an RMSE of 0.70 compared to 4.36. Both metrics agree.

### Diebold-Mariano test (5.2)

```{r}
errs <- gas_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(can_gas) |> select(Month, actual = Volume), by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) |>
  na.omit()

forecast::dm.test(errs$snaive, errs$tslm, h = 1, power = 1)
```

5.2a: The DM statistic is -31.28 and the p-value is less than 2.2e-16. So we reject that the two models are equally accurate, and the seasonal naive model is significantly better.

### Rolling window (5.3)

```{r}
gas_cv_fc_roll <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  slide_tsibble(.size = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc_roll |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |>
  select(.model, MAE, RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

5.3a: The TSLM changed a lot more. Its MAE went from 4.01 to 2.09 and its RMSE from 4.36 to 2.42, while the seasonal naive model stayed the same. This is because the trend isn't a straight line (like we saw in 4.4b), so using only the last 20 years lets the TSLM fit the more recent trend better. The seasonal naive model only uses the value from 12 months ago, so the window size doesn't affect it.

## Reflection

The residuals from the trend and seasonal dummies model still had a lot of pattern left in them. They moved in long waves and were highly correlated with past residuals, so one month's error told you a lot about the next month's. This is probably because the real trend bends over time and the seasonal swings change size, but the model assumes a straight line and the same seasonal effect every year. That also explains why the seasonal naive model did so much better in the forecast evaluation, since it uses recent data. A better model would probably use past values or past errors of the series to make forecasts, so it could pick up the pattern left in the residuals.
